1. PREMISE: Your framing treats his post-sexual silence and subsequent apology as symptoms of a single injury—the friendship's death—when they are separate violations with opposite moral content. The hidden assumption is that an apology following ghosting can repair the credibility damage of the ghosting itself. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that silence after intimacy and an apology for that silence operate in different registers: one destroys trust in his character, the other attempts to restore it, and no apology reaches backward to undo the first act's corrosive effect on your safety.

2. STAKES: You stand to lose the possibility of understanding why he disappeared, which affects your ability to assess whether the relationship carried hidden dangers you did not detect, and whether you can trust your own judgment about people close to you. He stands to lose access to your presence and conversation, which matters to him as shown by his monitoring. The friendship as it existed stands to be dissolved or fundamentally altered. Your capacity to process betrayal by someone positioned as protective—he was the person who supported you through abuse—stands to be either integrated into a revised understanding of him or left as unresolved injury.

3. DIRECTIVE: Do not accept or reciprocate contact until you have stated to him in writing, before any conversation occurs, what behavior you require going forward and what his silence cost you. The decisive reason is that meeting him on his schedule, with his apology as the opening move, allows him to control the terms on which trust is rebuilt and cedes to him the power to define whether his actions warrant your continued presence.

[Rejected path: Accept his apology and resume friendship at a reduced intensity. This produces a situation in which you remain unable to distinguish between genuine change in his behavior and his learned ability to manage your response; probability of primary harm: high.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Communicate directly to him that resumed contact requires him to explain without deflection what motivated his withdrawal and why he allowed weeks to pass without addressing the damage. His failure to offer reasons in his initial apology is itself data: it suggests either that he cannot articulate his motives or that he is unwilling to face scrutiny. The mechanism by which an unexplained apology fails is that it asks you to forgive an action whose nature remains obscure, which means you cannot evaluate whether the same action will recur. The competing view—that accepting his apology now preserves the friendship and leaves room for later conversation—is outweighed by the fact that a friendship built on your willingness to absorb harm without explanation is not a friendship but a structure that permits him to harm you repeatedly. Therefore: write to him stating that you will not resume contact until he has explained, in detail and without prompting, why he withdrew after the sexual encounter and why he waited weeks before attempting to reconnect.
